text: MACHINE LEARNING WITH GRAPHS · FINAL PRESENTATION
Does user–item graph information improve a generative recommender? Our methods, results and conclusions.
notes: Hello Everyone,
Our project investigates whether information from a user–item graph can improve generative recommendation.

We use Amazon Beauty purchase histories to predict a user’s next product. We compare three ways of incorporating graph information: re-ranking recommendations, changing the item codes, and enriching the recommender’s input.
We’ll cover these approaches, and present the results from our two experimental stages.

text: Can a graph improve a generative recommender?
Given a user's past purchases on Amazon Beauty, recommend their next one.
It writes item codes built from product text, and never sees who bought what.
We tested three places to add LightGCN's user–item signal: A, B and C.
Stage 1: full Amazon Beauty (147k users, 163k items).  Stage 2: the papers' 5-core version (22k users, 12k items).  Metrics: Recall and NDCG at 10.
notes: The task is next-item recommendation: given a user’s purchase history, predict the next product they will interact with.

TIGER represents products using short codes derived from product information. Its recommendation model does learn from purchase sequences, so it already receives interaction information. Our question is whether an explicit graph representation provides useful additional information beyond those sequences.
We study this in two settings: a larger project dataset with approximately 147,000 users, and the smaller 5-core Beauty dataset used in the paper-based experiments.
For comparison, We use Recall@10, which measures whether the target appears in the top ten recommendations, and NDCG@10 (Non Discounted Cumulative Gain), which also rewards placing it higher.

text: Where the graph can enter the recommender
Add graph to the item input
notes: This diagram separates item representation from recommendation.
First, we encode product text and convert the resulting vectors into discrete semantic IDs. The recommender then reads a user’s history through these item representations and predicts the next item.
We test three insertion points for graph information.

Method A uses graph scores to re-rank candidates after TIGER has generated them. Method B combines text and graph vectors before quantization, changing the semantic IDs themselves. Method C preserves text-derived codes and adds graph information to the continuous input of the recommendation model.
These approaches let us investigate whether the point of integration matters.

text: Every product gets a short code from its text
RQ-VAE and RK-Means: pick the closest of 256 centres, subtract, repeat 3 times (4 tokens). OPQ (for RPG): cut the vector into 32 pieces (32 tokens).
Products with similar text share the first numbers.
No purchase data is used here.
notes: Semantic IDs represent an item with several discrete tokens instead of a single catalog identifier.
For TIGER, we use three quantization levels, each with 256 possible codes, followed by a collision token that distinguishes items sharing the same three-code prefix.

RQ-VAE learns a neural representation and quantizes it through successive residual steps. Residual k-means also quantizes successive residuals, but fits cluster centers without a neural encoder and decoder. It still requires fitting; it is not training-free.
For our RPG-style model, we use optimized product quantization, or OPQ, to produce 32 code tokens. OPQ learns a rotation and quantizes separate vector subspaces.
These codes capture aspects of embedding similarity, but similar products are not guaranteed to share a prefix. In the baseline and Method C, the codes come from text alone.

text: TIGER writes the next item's code, token by token
Predicts the next item's code tokens.
It never sees who bought what.
notes: TIGER uses a T5 encoder–decoder architecture. The encoder reads up to twenty previous items represented by their semantic IDs. The decoder predicts the next item’s code one token at a time.
Training uses observed interaction sequences, with the next item’s code as the target. The additional information we introduce is a separately learned graph representation.
At inference, beam search generates candidate codes, which are mapped back to products.

(can skip) Our two stages use different decoding settings: stage one uses constrained beam search with thirty candidates, while the paper-protocol stage uses unconstrained beam search with beam size twenty. That distinction matters when interpreting results across the two stages.

text: LightGCN turns purchases into item vectors
Trained with BPR: a bought item should score higher than a random unbought one.
Items bought by the same people get similar vectors.
No weights to learn per layer
Only the start vectors are trained.
Test purchases never enter the graph.
notes: LightGCN represents users and products as nodes in a bipartite graph, with training interactions forming the edges.

Each node starts with a trainable embedding. Two propagation rounds combine neighboring embeddings using degree-normalized weights. The final representation averages the initial embedding and the outputs from both rounds.
The model is trained with a pairwise ranking objective that encourages observed interactions to score above sampled unobserved interactions.
LightGCN has no learned transformation matrix at each propagation layer; the initial embeddings are the trainable parameters.
We use training edges to construct the graph. The final stage-one experiments use 768-dimensional embeddings, while the stage-two graph model uses 64 dimensions.

text: TIGER is used as it is.
A good first test of the graph.
notes: So now that we understand TIGER and LightGCN individually, our next question was: how can we actually combine them?
We started with probably the simplest approach, which is re-ranking.
The idea here is that we don't want to modify TIGER's architecture or retrain it. We simply want to see whether LightGCN can improve the recommendations TIGER is already generating.
So if you look at the diagram, the first part is exactly the same as our original TIGER model.
We give TIGER a user's purchase history, and instead of immediately taking its top 10 recommendations, we ask it to generate 30 candidate products.
Now, these 30 products are selected based on what TIGER has learned from purchase sequences and the semantic representations of items.
But we also have LightGCN, which has learned something different. It understands the user–item interaction graph, meaning which users have interacted with which products.
So for each of these 30 candidates, we calculate a graph score using the dot product of the user's LightGCN embedding and the candidate item's embedding.
Let me give you an example.
Suppose TIGER recommends a particular face cream at position 8, but LightGCN gives it a high score because users with similar purchasing behavior have frequently bought that cream.
We can use this additional graph information to move that product higher in the recommendation list.
But there is one fundamental limitation.
Suppose the actual product the user purchases next isn't even among TIGER's top 30 candidates. LightGCN cannot recover it because it never gets the opportunity to score that product.
So this approach can improve the ranking of existing candidates, but it cannot change which candidates TIGER generates.
And that's what motivated our next approach.

text: METHODOLOGY 5 · METHOD B · GRAPH IN THE CODES
B: mix the graph into the vector we quantize
notes: So with our first method, we realized that graph information was only being introduced at the very end.
But what if we introduce it much earlier?
More specifically, what if the semantic IDs themselves contain information about user–item interactions?
That's exactly what we investigate in Method B.
Remember, in our original TIGER architecture, every product is represented using a Sentence-T5 embedding, which is based on textual information such as the product title, brand, and category.
But textual similarity and collaborative similarity aren't necessarily the same thing.
For example, consider two products: a sunscreen and a moisturizer.
Their descriptions might be quite different, so their text embeddings might not be particularly close.
But suppose many users who buy this sunscreen also buy that moisturizer.
From a recommendation perspective, there is a meaningful relationship between those two products, even though their descriptions don't necessarily capture it.
And this is precisely the kind of relationship that LightGCN can learn.
So instead of generating semantic IDs using only the text embedding, we now take two representations.
The first is our text embedding, which we call c, and the second is our graph embedding from LightGCN, which we call g.
We combine these two representations into a single vector, and then pass that vector through RQ-VAE to generate new semantic IDs.
The important difference is that the quantizer is now working with both semantic information and collaborative information.
First, we tried simple addition.
Here, we normalize the embeddings and add them together. It's a very direct approach, where both signals contribute to the resulting representation.
Second, we tried concatenation.
Instead of adding the embeddings, we place them next to each other. This allows us to preserve information from both representations without immediately mixing their individual dimensions.
Third, we tried an MLP.

The idea here is that maybe the relationship between textual information and graph information is nonlinear. So instead of manually deciding how to combine them, we use a small neural network to learn a fused representation.
Fourth, we introduced a learned scalar.
Here, rather than assuming that text and graph information should contribute equally, we learn a parameter controlling the contribution of the graph embedding.
And finally, we tried a learned gate.
This is a more adaptive approach, where the model can assign different contributions to the graph signal for different items.
Once we have these fused vectors, we quantize them into semantic IDs and train TIGER using the new IDs.
So the TIGER architecture remains unchanged, but the actual item representation is different, and we retrain the recommender with these new representations.
One important detail is that these fusion mechanisms are fitted separately before quantization. They aren't jointly trained with the final TIGER recommendation model.
Method B changes the representation of the products themselves. Unlike re-ranking, it can influence which items TIGER learns to generate, but the quality of quantization becomes very important.

text: RPG predicts a long code all at once
All 32 tokens predicted in one step.
Beats TIGER; base for method C.
notes: Recommendation with Parallel semantic ID Generation
So far, we've been working primarily with TIGER.
But for the second stage of our experiments, we also wanted to investigate whether graph information could improve a stronger generative recommendation architecture.
That's where RPG comes in.
The overall goal is still the same: given a user's purchase history, predict the next item.
But RPG takes a different approach to representing and predicting products.
Let me first compare it with TIGER.
In TIGER, we typically have four code tokens representing an item, and the decoder predicts them sequentially.
So it predicts the first token, then the second token conditioned on the first, and so on.
In our RPG-style architecture, we're instead using 32 code tokens per item, generated using optimized product quantization.
But just having more tokens isn't the most important difference.
The real difference is how the model predicts those tokens.
Rather than generating all 32 sequentially, the model predicts the 32 code positions in parallel.
Now, let's follow the diagram.
First, we have the user's interaction history, where every item is represented by 32 code tokens.
We take the learned embeddings of those tokens and average them to obtain one continuous embedding for each history item.
So even though the item is represented by 32 discrete tokens, the recommendation model receives a single continuous item representation.
These representations are then passed into a two-layer GPT-style decoder, which learns patterns across the user's previous interactions.
At the output, we have 32 prediction heads, one for each position in the item's code.
Each head predicts the possible token values for its corresponding position.
In our implementation, we then score the items in the catalog using these token predictions and select the top 10 recommendations.
Now, there's a very important reason why we introduced this architecture.
Look at this continuous item embedding.
This gives us another opportunity to integrate graph information.
Instead of modifying the discrete semantic IDs, what if we directly enrich the continuous representation that the recommendation model receives?
That leads us to our third method, which is actually the most important one.

text: METHODOLOGY 7 · METHOD C · GATED INPUT FUSION
C: a gated graph signal in the input
The graph never touches the quantizer.
The gate goes to 0 where the graph doesn't help.
notes: But in Method C, we wanted to preserve the original semantic IDs and introduce graph information directly into the recommendation model.
Let me explain why.
When we put graph information into the semantic IDs, we're forcing two different kinds of information into a single discrete representation.
And once that representation is quantized, some information is inevitably lost.
So we asked ourselves: why not let the recommendation model learn how much graph information it actually needs?
That's the idea behind gated input fusion.
If you follow the diagram, we first have our 32 code tokens representing a product.
We average their learned token embeddings to obtain the continuous item representation, which we're calling e.
Separately, we have the pretrained LightGCN representation, which we're calling g.
But instead of directly adding this projected graph vector, we introduce a gate.
The gate produces weights between zero and one, controlling how much graph information contributes to each dimension of the input representation.
So our final item representation becomes:"
\[ \boxed{h=e+\operatorname{gate}(e,g)\odot(Pg)} \]
"Here, e represents what we've learned from the item's semantic codes.
P times g is the projected LightGCN embedding.
And the gate controls how much of that graph representation we add.
Let me give you an intuitive example.
Suppose a user frequently purchases products from a particular skincare brand.
We might have two products with very similar descriptions, so their semantic embeddings are also similar.
But from the purchase graph, LightGCN may recognize that one of those products is much more strongly associated with users who have purchasing patterns similar to this user.
By incorporating graph information into the item representation, the recommender has the opportunity to use that relationship when predicting the next item.
And the important part is that we're not fixing the graph contribution manually.
The gate and projection are learned during the recommendation model's training.
So the model can learn different amounts of graph contribution across embedding dimensions.
One thing I want to distinguish from Method B is that even though both methods involve a learned gate, they aren't doing the same thing.
In Method B, the gate is trained before quantization, and its output changes the discrete semantic IDs.
In Method C, the gate is trained jointly with the actual recommendation objective, and the semantic IDs remain text-derived.
The pretrained LightGCN embeddings stay frozen, but the gate and projection learn along with the recommender.
And that difference is important because the graph signal is now being optimized for the recommendation task itself.
So our hypothesis was that this could provide a more flexible way of integrating collaborative information without disturbing the semantic ID structure.
And as we'll see in our second-stage results, this is where we observed our most consistent improvement.

text: RESULTS · STAGE 1 · 147,241 USERS, ONE SEED EACH
Stage 1: the graph adds 2–4% at best
More graph in the codes, lower recall: 0.0594 → 0.0530 as the graph weight goes 0.25 → 2.
notes: On the larger project dataset, text-only TIGER achieves Recall@10 of approximately 0.0334, about 4.1 times the popularity baseline.

The bars show relative changes in NDCG@10. MLP fusion improves it by approximately 3.9%, fixed addition by 3.3%, and re-ranking by 2.2%. The learned gate applied before quantization reduces performance by approximately 7.9%.

These are single-seed experiments. The bootstrap analysis measures variation across test users, not variation across training seeds, and its reported significance tests are uncorrected for multiple comparisons. The fixed-addition gain also becomes less convincing when we restrict it to the baseline’s training budget.
The 5-core code-fusion experiments are mixed: a small graph weight can help, while larger weights often hurt. They do not show a strictly monotonic decline.
The evidence therefore motivates testing another integration point rather than concluding that graph information is inherently unsuitable for codes.

text: The graph helps rare items, not cold ones
TEST TARGETS, BY HOW OFTEN THE ITEM WAS BOUGHT IN TRAINING
Recall@10 for every model. No purchases, so the graph has nothing to add.
Recall@10 0.0003 → 0.0016 with the graph. Clear gain, still tiny.
Recall@10, about equal for all models. These set the overall score.
notes: We divide stage-one test targets by how often they appeared in training.
Approximately 20.7% have no training interactions. Recall is effectively zero for these cold items across the evaluated methods. These experiments do not solve the cold-start problem.

Another 25.2% have between one and four training interactions. Fixed-addition fusion increases Recall@10 from approximately 0.00030 to 0.00156—about a 5.3-fold improvement using the unrounded values. That is a large relative gain, but the absolute recall remains very low.

The remaining 54.1% have at least five training interactions and account for most successful recommendations. Several methods perform similarly on this group, although the learned code-fusion gate performs noticeably worse.
The benefit depends on both the fusion method and item frequency.

text: RESULTS · STAGE 2 · 5-CORE BEAUTY, THE PAPERS' SETTING
notes: Stage two uses 5-core Beauty, with 22,363 users and 12,101 items.
We examine three questions: how closely we reproduce TIGER, whether graph information improves the RPG-style model, and whether stronger text encoders offer an additional benefit.

Our TIGER results are 0.0546 Recall@10 with RQ-VAE and 0.0583 with residual k-means. Official RPG with Sentence-T5 reaches 0.0736, while our RPG-style baseline reaches 0.0725. Adding gated LightGCN raises our baseline to 0.0767.
The updated Qwen results are 0.0739 for Qwen3 8B without the graph and 0.0775 for Qwen3 4B with the gate.

These comparisons still require care. Published results use different embedding or implementation choices. Our two stages also differ in evaluation: stage one masks previously seen items, while stage two does not.

text: Our TIGER reaches about 85% of the paper
Test Recall@10 by type of item ID (paper's own ablation)
SAME GAP FOR EVERY ID TYPE
So the gap is in T5 training details the paper leaves out, not in our codes.
RK-Means in place of RQ-VAE, with nothing to train. Seven other fixes failed.
notes: Our RQ-VAE-based TIGER reaches approximately 85% of the published three-seed Recall@10.

We also examine random and locality-sensitive hashing IDs. These variants fall below their published reference values as well. This suggests that factors beyond the RQ-VAE tokenizer may contribute to the reproduction gap, but it does not establish the exact cause.
The comparison is exploratory because the random and hashing experiments use one seed, while the main RQ-VAE result averages three seeds.

Replacing RQ-VAE with residual k-means increases Recall@10 from 0.0546 to 0.0583, approximately a 6.7% relative improvement. Residual k-means still requires fitting its cluster centers, but avoids neural autoencoder training.
Several additional training and architecture changes were tested without closing the gap. We therefore report a partial reproduction and keep the remaining discrepancy explicit.

text: STAGE 2 · 2 · GRAPH IN THE INPUT (METHOD C)
Test Recall@10 per training seed, RPG-style model
Above official RPG with the same encoder (0.0736)
notes: This is our strongest result.
We compare the RPG-style model with and without gated LightGCN using the same six training seeds. The gated model improves Recall@10 in all six.

Mean Recall@10 increases from 0.0725 to 0.0767, a relative improvement of approximately 5.8%. The paired test gives a p-value of approximately 0.0014. NDCG@10 increases by approximately 4.3%, with a p-value of approximately 0.014.
The gated model’s mean also exceeds our official RPG baseline using the same text encoder, although the six-seed significance result specifically concerns our matched baseline comparison.
The gate and projection add approximately 1.9% to the recommender’s trainable parameters. That figure excludes the separately trained LightGCN model and its computational cost.
A scalar fusion variant reaches 0.0758 across three seeds. Its lower mean is suggestive, but does not establish that the gate is reliably better.

text: The graph gains more than a bigger text encoder
Test Recall@10, RPG-style model (axis starts at 0.070)
notes: We now have results for Qwen3 encoders at several sizes and for BGE-large.
Without graph input, Qwen3 0.6B and BGE-large perform close to Sentence-T5. Qwen3 4B and 8B both reach approximately 0.0739 Recall@10.
For Qwen3 8B, that is about 2% above the six-seed Sentence-T5 mean. Comparing only matching seeds gives approximately 1.7%, and the difference is not statistically significant in the available runs.
With gated LightGCN, Qwen3 4B reaches 0.0775 across three seeds, while Qwen3 8B reaches 0.0765 across four. Sentence-T5 with the gate reaches 0.0767 across six.

Qwen3 4B has the highest numerical Recall@10 among these encoder variants, but its advantage over the gated Sentence-T5 model is not statistically established. Both gated Qwen variants have NDCG@10 of approximately 0.0436.
The graph improvement has stronger experimental support than the additional benefit from increasing encoder size.

text: A learned gate on each item's input: +5.8% Recall@10, 6 of 6 seeds.
Graph in the codes gave 2–4% at best on full data, and hurt on 5-core.
Worth more than a Qwen3 8B encoder; together, our best: 0.0778.
Close the gap to published RPG (0.0809)
More seeds for the best setup
notes: Our clearest finding is that gated graph input improves the RPG-style model on 5-core Beauty: approximately 5.8% higher Recall@10, with improvements across all six matched seeds.

Graph information inside the semantic IDs produces smaller and less consistent benefits. For our current configuration, text-derived codes combined with graph-enriched inputs are the best-supported choice.
Larger text encoders do not yet demonstrate a reliable additional gain once the graph gate is included.

We also tested ACERec-style token merging, intent tokens, and alignment losses. These were single-seed experiments using our own reimplementation. They did not improve Recall@10 over the gated RPG-style baseline, although one gated variant achieved higher NDCG@10. They therefore warrant a qualified conclusion rather than a claim that every component fails.

Next steps include tuning the gated model, testing alternative graph representations, expanding matched-seed comparisons, and measuring training and inference costs. Cold-item performance also remains unresolved, particularly in the larger stage-one dataset.
